questions.q: Electricity use that is normal in May in Chennai shows up in January. What kind of anomaly is this?
options: A point anomaly
A collective anomaly
A contextual anomaly
Not an anomaly, because the value has been seen before
questions.why: The value is only odd in its context (the season). A point anomaly is extreme on its own, and a collective anomaly is a group of individually normal points that is odd together, such as fifty small transfers to one new account. Having seen a value before does not make it normal in every context.

questions.q: What does the `contamination` parameter of scikit-learn's Isolation Forest do?
options: Removes that share of points from the training data before fitting
Sets the number of trees in the forest
Changes how the anomaly scores are calculated
Sets the threshold so that roughly that share of training points is flagged, without changing the scores
questions.why: Contamination only decides where the cut-off falls on the score scale; the ranking of points stays the same. Guessing it badly (say 5% when the true rate is 0.1%) floods the team with alerts, so a threshold based on review capacity is often better.

questions.q: A customer's transactions have mean ₹1,285 and standard deviation ₹377. A new transaction of ₹2,400 arrives. What is its z-score, and does the |z| > 3 rule flag it?
options: z ≈ 2.96, not flagged
z ≈ 1.87, not flagged
z ≈ 2.96, flagged
z ≈ 3.50, flagged
questions.why: z = (2,400 − 1,285) / 377 ≈ 2.96, just under 3, so the rule does not flag it. 1.87 is 2,400 / 1,285, a ratio rather than a distance in standard deviations; 3.50 is the value for ₹2,600. A hard cut-off means amounts just either side of it are treated very differently.

questions.q: Daily support tickets have Q1 = 40 and Q3 = 64. Using the IQR rule, what is the upper fence above which a day is flagged?
questions.why: IQR = 64 − 40 = 24, and the upper fence = Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 64 + 36 = 100. 88 forgets the 1.5 multiplier (Q3 + IQR), and 96 multiplies Q3 by 1.5 instead of the IQR.

questions.q: An Isolation Forest uses sub-samples of 256, so c(256) ≈ 10.24. A transaction has an average path length of 5. Using score = 2^(−E[h(x)] / c(n)), what is its anomaly score?
questions.why: 2^(−5 / 10.24) = 2^(−0.488) ≈ 0.71, fairly anomalous (scores near 1 are anomalies; about 0.5 or below are normal). 0.49 is just the ratio 5 / 10.24, 0.29 is 1 minus the score, and 0.82 is the score for a path length of 3.

questions.q: A ₹48,000 transaction was accidentally left in the history used to compute the mean and standard deviation. Its own z-score is now only about 3.01. What is happening?
options: ₹48,000 is genuinely not very unusual for this customer
The sample is too small to compute a z-score
Masking: the outlier inflates both the mean and the SD, so it hides itself; use the median and MAD (robust z) or a clean baseline
The z-score rule should be lowered to |z| > 2
questions.why: One extreme value drags the mean up and the SD way up, shrinking its own z-score (with 11 values no z-score can exceed about 3.02). The median (₹1,300) and MAD (₹350) are not moved, giving a robust z of about 90. Lowering the cut-off would just add false alarms elsewhere.

questions.q: Interview: "Every year your anomaly detector floods the team with alerts in Diwali week. How would you fix it?"
options: Raise the contamination parameter for the whole year
Delete Diwali weeks from the training data
Switch off the detector during festivals
Treat seasonality as normal: add calendar and festival features, detect anomalies on residuals after removing the seasonal pattern, or compare with the same period last year
questions.why: A predictable spike is not an anomaly; the model just does not know about the calendar. Giving it that context removes the false alarms while keeping it alert during the busiest, most fraud-prone weeks. Deleting festival weeks from training would make them look even stranger.

questions.q: The overall fraud rate is 0.2%. Analysts review the 200 highest-scoring transactions and confirm 30 as fraud. What is precision at 200, and how many times richer in fraud is the queue than random checking?
options: 15%, about 7.5 times richer
15%, about 75 times richer
30%, about 150 times richer
99.8%, because almost all transactions are correctly left alone
questions.why: Precision@200 = 30 / 200 = 15%; random checking would find 0.2%, and 15% / 0.2% = 75. The 99.8% option is the accuracy trap: a detector that never raises an alert would score that too, which is why accuracy is useless for rare events.
